case_studies.title: An Organization-Scoped LLM Agent Runtime Architecture for Regulated Cybersecurity Operations
case_studies.abstract: Regulated cybersecurity workflows lack a runtime substrate that enforces organization-level scope across retrieval, tool calls, memory, findings, reports, and audit while remaining model-agnostic and locally deployable. Recent large language model (LLM) agent systems report strong results on isolated cybersecurity tasks, yet they do not by themselves define an auditable platform architecture for regulated security operations centre (SOC) and compliance workflows, where a single analyst may trigger actions that bind the organization, and where the runtime must integrate with existing SIEM/XDR s
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of lacking a runtime substrate for regulated cybersecurity operations by building an organization-scoped LLM agent runtime architecture, resulting in an auditable platform for security operations centre and compliance workflows. The architecture enforces organization-level scope and is model-agnostic and locally deployable. It aims to integrate with existing SIEM/XDR systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage security operations centre infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current architecture for potential integration with the proposed LLM agent runtime, check if your existing SIEM/XDR systems are compatible, and assess the potential benefits of implementing this architecture for regulated cybersecurity operations.
case_studies.relevance_tag: regulated cybersecurity operations, LLMs, auditable platform architecture
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a runtime architecture for regulated cybersecurity operations, leveraging LLMs in a real-world scenario. IT engineers might find it relevant for understanding how to deploy LLMs in regulated environments, but its novelty and impact are somewhat contained within the field. An IT engineer could potentially use this to propose a service to clients within 90 days, but the specifics are left up to interpretation.

case_studies.title: Investigating Detection and Obfuscation of Prompt Injection Attacks Against Software Reverse Engineering AI Agents
case_studies.abstract: Agentic software reverse engineering systems are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks placed into the source code of executable binary files. This research demonstrates defensive tactics for detecting the presences of prompt injection strings in the decompiler output of adversarial example programs. Methods for obfuscating these attacks and subsequent methods for defending against these obfuscations are also explored. This research advances the understanding of risk and security of agentic software analysis systems necessary for their deployment into production-level cyber workflows.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of prompt injection attacks against software reverse engineering AI agents by detecting and defending against these attacks. The researchers built defensive tactics to detect and obfuscate prompt injection strings in decompiler output. The result is an improved understanding of the risks and security of agentic software analysis systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered software reverse engineering systems, here is what to do: review your system's decompiler output for signs of prompt injection attacks, check for obfuscated code, and implement defensive tactics to prevent these attacks. This flags a risk: if your org uses AI agents for software analysis, check your systems immediately for potential vulnerabilities. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those using AI-powered software analysis tools.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 5, IT Relevance: 6, Value: 6. The novelty is high because this paper shows surprising vulnerabilities in AI systems commonly used by IT engineers. IT Relevance is high because it affects how IT engineers work, particularly in the context of reverse engineering and AI security. Value is moderate because while the suggestions for defensive tactics and methods for obfuscation are actionable, they're more applicable to the development of security products rather than immediate implementation in existing workflows.

case_studies.title: Certified Policy Optimisation for Nested Causal Bandits via PAC-Bayes Risk
case_studies.abstract: Critical sequential decisions are rarely single-timescale: a strategic decision causally shapes the context in which every subsequent tactical choice is made; standard bandit and reinforcement-learning theory does not capture this causal coupling between timescales. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of making sequential decisions in complex environments where strategic and tactical choices are causally linked, by building a framework called Nested Contextual Causal Bandits and an algorithm called Nested Causal Thompson Sampling, which results in more effective decision-making. The outcome is a theoretical framework for optimising policy decisions in nested causal bandit problems. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Memory-Bound but Not Bandwidth-Limited: The Physical AI Inference Gap in Batch-1 LLM Decode
case_studies.abstract: Physical AI systems, including robots, autonomous vehicles, embodied agents and edge copilots, often run a different inference workload from cloud LLM serving: single-stream, batch-1 autoregressive decode, where one robot, camera feed or user session waits on the next token. This workload is usually described as memory-bandwidth-bound. Each decode step streams model weights and the active KV cache, so latency should scale with peak HBM bandwidth. We show that this account is true but incomplete. We measure batch-1 decode for three 7 to 8B-class GQA transformers across four NVIDIA GPUs: H100 SX
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of optimizing AI inference in physical systems, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, by investigating the limitations of batch-1 autoregressive decode. The researchers built a measurement system to test the performance of three large language models on four NVIDIA GPUs. The result shows that the current understanding of this workload is incomplete, and latency does not scale solely with peak HBM bandwidth.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered edge devices or robots, here is what to do: review your current GPU configuration, check if your workload is memory-bandwidth-bound, and consider optimizing your model weights and active KV cache for better performance. This flags a risk: if your organization uses NVIDIA GPUs for AI inference, check your current HBM bandwidth utilization immediately. Not directly applicable to cloud infrastructure work, but relevant to edge computing and IoT devices.
